n: Isaiah 3 warns that the Lord will take away Judah’s support — its “stay and staff,” meaning its food, water, and leaders. This came true during sieges by Assyria and Babylon.

f.g: Support and supply; everything they lean on.

n: He will remove warriors, judges, prophets, wise men, and elders — the people society depends on.
Military captains, nobles, counselors, skilled craftsmen, and gifted speakers will also be removed. Babylon later deported exactly these kinds of people.

f.g: A military officer over fifty soldiers.

n: With capable leaders gone, immature and inexperienced people — “children” — will rule.
Society will break down: neighbors oppress neighbors, the young defy the old, and the lowly insult the honorable.
Things get so bad that a man will beg his relative to lead simply because he owns a cloak.

f.w: Thou hast clothing, be thou our ruler
f.g: Even minimal resources seem like qualifications to lead.

n: The relative will refuse: he can’t heal the nation’s wounds, for he has no food or clothing either.

f.w: I will not be a healer

n: Jerusalem and Judah collapse because their words and actions defy the Lord.

f.w: to provoke the eyes of his glory
f.g: To openly defy God in His very presence.

n: Their faces show their guilt. Like Sodom, they don’t even hide their sin. In harming others, they have really harmed themselves.

f.w: they have rewarded evil unto themselves

n: Tell the righteous it will go well with them — they will enjoy the fruits of their good deeds.

f.w: they shall eat the fruit of their doings

n: Woe to the wicked; they will receive what their own hands have done.
God laments that His people are oppressed by immature leaders and misled by those who should guide them.

f.w: they who lead thee cause thee to err

n: The Lord rises like a judge in a courtroom to plead His case against the people.

f.w: The Lord standeth up to plead

n: He brings charges against Judah’s elders and princes: they have devoured the vineyard (God’s people) and stored the plunder taken from the poor in their houses.

f.w: ye have eaten up the vineyard

n: “What do you mean by crushing my people and grinding the faces of the poor?” God takes oppression of the poor personally.

f.w: grind the faces of the poor

n: Isaiah now condemns the proud “daughters of Zion,” the wealthy women of Jerusalem, who strut with raised necks, flirtatious eyes, and jingling ankle ornaments. Their vanity symbolizes the whole nation’s pride.
Their pride will be replaced with disease and humiliation — the fate of captives in war.
Isaiah lists the finery that will be stripped away: anklets, hairnets, and crescent-shaped ornaments.
Necklaces, bracelets, and veils.
Headdresses, ankle chains, sashes, perfume boxes, and charms.
Rings and nose rings.
Festive robes, cloaks, shawls, and purses.

f.g: Purses or bags (KJV guessed hair-curling pins).

n: Mirrors, fine linen, turbans, and veils. The long list shows how much they had invested in appearance.
Every symbol of luxury will be reversed: perfume to stench, sash to rope, styled hair to baldness, fine robes to sackcloth, and beauty to branding — the treatment of captives.

f.g: A rich robe or ornamented garment.
Possibly branding, a mark of slavery.

n: Jerusalem’s men will die in battle.

f.w: Thy men shall fall by the sword

n: Jerusalem is pictured as a widow sitting on the ground at her gates, mourning and empty — a scene fulfilled when Babylon destroyed the city.
